Googlebook — a new category of laptops designed for the way we work today — is now available for pre-order. Built on the Android technology stack and paired with desktop foundations from ChromeOS, Googlebook is designed for Gemini Intelligence and engineered to work with your Android phone right out of the box.

Today, we often switch between starting tasks on our phones and finishing them on our laptops. To make that experience better for Android users, we teamed up with the best laptop makers in the industry to deliver top-tier hardware alongside Google software that connects effortlessly with your phone.
Premium hardware from leading partners

Our initial selection of flagship devices are built by Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, and Lenovo, offering you choices that fit your style.

Starting at $899, every Googlebook features premium materials like aluminum, magnesium alloy, and carbon fiber. You’ll find responsive touchscreens with up to 2.8K OLED displays, haptic glass trackpads, and backlit keyboards. Under the hood, top-of-the-line processors from Intel and Qualcomm — paired with dedicated NPUs capable of over 45 TOPS — deliver snappy on-device performance and up to 14 hours of battery life.

We’re also bringing back a familiar favorite: the Glowbar. Positioned cleanly on the exterior, it lights up at startup, sweeps to show your battery charge level, and reacts with playful animations when you talk to Gemini.
The companion your phone has been waiting for
Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos, but don't worry, you can and watch it with your favorite video player!
If you use an Android phone, your laptop shouldn't treat it like a stranger. Googlebook is built on a shared Android foundation, so your phone and laptop work seamlessly together

It starts with setting up your device. When you sign in, your Android phone’s settings, saved passwords, Wi-Fi networks, and messages will move with you, backed by end-to-end encryption. Once you’re set up, Googlebook makes it easy to move between your phone and laptop and back to get things done.

Continue On: Pick up exactly where you left off on your phone, right on your laptop. If you start a project in BandLab on your phone while commuting, you can open your Googlebook and continue right from the taskbar.
    Files: Rather than hunting through downloads or emailing attachments to yourself, use your Googlebook’s Files app to view, search, and open files and photos from your phone.
    Cast My Apps: Need to order dinner from a delivery app or grab a one-time code from Messages? Cast My Apps lets you stream and interact with your phone’s apps in a desktop window without interrupting your workflow.
Helpful intelligence built into the desktop
Googlebook is designed for Gemini Intelligence to simplify your workflow.

Magic Pointer: Wiggle your cursor to bring Gemini directly to whatever’s on your screen. You can ask Gemini to organize a messy calendar or translate text without juggling multiple windows. Gemini only acts when you ask it to, and you can switch it off whenever you want.
    Rambler: Located right next to the Quick Insert key, Rambler turns spoken thoughts into organized, ready-to-share writing. Talk through your notes, action items, or a stream of consciousness — even in multiple languages — and Rambler structures them with clean headers, checklists, and formatted takeaways.
    Create My Widget: Customize your desktop by describing what you need in plain language.
Create My Widget generates custom widgets that can share relevant updates throughout your day.

The full web, plus your favorite apps and tools
CapCut on the Googlebook
Googlebook brings together the best of the web and the Play Store.
You get the desktop-class Chrome browser with extensions alongside millions of Android apps, many of them optimized for large screens, mouse and keyboard input.

Run native creative tools like Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Lightroom, and CapCut, or watch shows on popular streaming platforms like Netflix and HBO Max with offline viewing supported. When it’s time to unwind, explore thousands of Android games or play AAA PC titles you own with a complimentary year of GeForce NOW included with every purchase.

For builders and makers, Googlebook includes Antigravity, our AI agent development platform, allowing you to build, test, and deploy apps right on your device. Developers also get a full terminal environment to run tools like Claude Code or Antigravity CLI and perform serious agentic coding.
Modern, secure software architecture

Googlebook is built on the same security architecture as ChromeOS, anchored with our Google Titan hardware root of trust, defense in-depth architecture, and on-device malware detection. This means you get the security of industry-leading protection for all your personal data from day one.

It also features a first for the laptop category: a Level 5 security-certified pKVM hypervisor. This hypervisor powers an isolated Linux environment with a full terminal access, so you can safely run any Linux developer tools, pull code repositories, or execute autonomous agents.
Pricing, availability, and pre-order details

Starting at $899, every Googlebook includes 12 months of Google AI Pro providing 5TB of cloud storage and higher usage limits in Gemini, plus 3 months of YouTube Premium, Adobe Photoshop, and more. Googlebook OS also comes with regular feature drops and updates for up to 10 years.

Pre-orders are now open on the Google Store, Best Buy, and other select retailers. Devices arrive on shelves starting October 4 in the U.S., and October 5 in Canada, the U.K., Ireland, France, Germany, and Australia.

The Googlebook is a laptop standard created by Google that runs an Android-based desktop operating system called "Googlebook OS". It was announced on May 12, 2026, as the successor to the Chromebook, and were first launched on October 4, 2026 with gradual global expansion.[2]
History

Google first confirmed it was developing a successor to the Chromebook and Pixelbook Go, a lineup of mid to low-range laptop computers that run ChromeOS popular in U.S. K–12 education, in July 2025, when executive Sameer Samat told TechRadar that it was "combining ChromeOS and Android into a single platform", confirming months-long rumors and fulfilling decade-long wishes.[3] He teased the new platform again in September, at Qualcomm's Snapdragon Summit event with Google hardware chief Rick Osterloh and Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, saying that it would be launched in the following year.[4]

In May 2026, at a livestreamed Google I/O pre-show entitled "The Android Show: I/O Edition", Google announced the Googlebook alongside Android 17, highlighting its deep integration with Gemini Intelligence—a slate of generative artificial intelligence (AI) features powered by Gemini—and revealing that the first devices in the product line would be available later that year.[5] The company declined to share the name of the operating system that powers Googlebooks but clarified that "Aluminium OS" was a codename during development and would not be the actual name.[6] Initial third-party original equipment manufacturer (OEM) partners included Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo; the Google Pixel t

eam declined to comment on whether they would develop their own Googlebooks. Senior director Alexander Kuscher told Wired that Googlebooks would "sit at the more premium end of the laptop market", contrasting Chromebooks,[5] which would continue to be supported post-launch.[6]

Google officially revealed the product on May 21, 2026. Initial media lift and preorders began on September 21, 2026.[7] It was then released in the United States on October 4, 2026, followed by Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Ireland and the United Kingdom the next day on October 5.[2]
Features

Googlebook is a computer platform with Googlebook OS, computer-class Arm64 or x64 SoC, UEFI boot, and NVMe storage.[8]
Reception
Upon Samat's confirmation in July 2025, PCMag reviewer Michael Muchmore expressed excitement for the ChromeOS–Android merger, calling it "the most logical path forward for Google".[9]

After first unveiling its new AI-powered laptop, dubbed Googlebook, in May, Google on Monday said the new device is now available for preorder for $899.

Meant to offer a step up from traditional Chromebooks, Googlebooks run on Android OS with a desktop version of the Chrome browser and other familiar ChromeOS elements. However, the real pull for the new devices is that they’ll prominently feature Gemini’s latest capabilities in a new format: the laptop.

Google is trying to offer a laptop with unique features like an AI-powered cursor, vibe-coded widgets, and support for AI-enhanced dictation. The latter is a feature called Rambler, which cleans up messy, rambling brain dumps into readable text.

The move is a bet that AI, specifically Google’s Gemini, could be enough of a draw to get people to buy a new laptop that bakes in AI instead of running them via desktop apps you install or access through the browser. In addition, the devices could eventually replace Chromebooks, bringing millions of former Chromebook customers to Gemini AI.

On the Googlebook, Google is trying to reinvent the “point-and-click” experience of desktop computing to now include an AI element: The cursor serves as a conduit to Gemini. The company suggests various ways this could be used, like highlighting content on a web page for Gemini to work with, asking Gemini to see if an email you’ve hovered your cursor over is suspicious, or selecting images and then asking Gemini to visualize them together.
Image Credits:Google

In practice, this feature isn’t very different from Android’s “Circle to Search,” which allows smartphone owners to use gestures like circling, highlighting, or tapping to connect with Google Search, which of course, also includes AI. While it’s a clever way to take advantage of the ways people use their phones, Circle to Search on its own didn’t inspire a mass exodus to Android.

Similarly, Magic Cursor, as the AI pointer is called, won’t likely be a main selling point for the Googlebook, especially now that we have AI agents that can take over your computer and browser to do tasks for you.

Google’s Rambler, however, may be one of the best of the AI features in this upgrade, as it meets a surprisingly useful need. However, this, too, isn’t enough reason to buy a new device, as it feels more like a feature that’s nice to have than a necessity.
Image Credits:Google
Vibe-coding widgets are a minor addition, as well. Other Googlebook features, like Gemini Spark and Gemini Live, also don’t require special, new hardware.

What’s more interesting about the Googlebook is how it’s seemingly part of Google’s longer-term plan to capture a large part of the K-12 market that currently relies on Chromebooks and push them toward the company’s Gemini AI. There are somewhere around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, Google has said.

In May, the company told TechCrunch that its current Chromebooks would continue to be supported, though many would become eligible to transition to the new Googlebook experience in the future.
Image Credits:Google

The $899 device will include 12 months of Google AI Pro, which gives you 5TB of cloud storage, Gemini Advanced tools, and 3 months of YouTube Premium, Adobe Photoshop, and more. The devices will receive regular updates for up to 10 years, Google said.

oogle’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out.

For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/$899/A$2,299) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks.

While Google does not make these machines directly, it has set strict hardware quality standards that the laptops must reach. That includes backlit keyboards, haptic trackpads, fingerprint readers, crisp touchscreens, decent speakers and modern fast chips with at least 16GB of RAM.

It is a list of specs you should expect with a premium Windows PC, but those start at a much higher price, primarily thanks to RAMageddon.
A pair of Acer and Asus Googlebooks sit side by side on a wooden table.
View image in fullscreen
The two Intel Core Ultra Series 3-powered Googlebooks on test: the Acer Googlebook 14 (left) and the Asus Googlebook 14 (right). Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The Guardian
As such, the Acer Googlebook 14 and the Asus Googlebook 14 I’ve been testing have excellent hardware with satisfying keyboards, great trackpads and quality screens.

The Acer is a convertible that allows the screen to fold over the back of the device turning into a tablet of sorts. It is 1.14kg and 13.9mm thick, with a glossy 14in 3K OLED screen and a smooth aluminium-magnesium body, costing £999.99.

The Asus is a traditional laptop with a matt 14in 3K OLED screen and a magnesium-alloy body that weighs just 0.99kg and is 11mm thick, costing £1,199.99.
Googlebook OS
A screenshot of Googlebook OS showing the desktop with widgets and the app drawer open from the taskbar.
View image in fullscreen
With an app drawer, widgets and a taskbar at the bottom, Googlebook OS looks a lot like ChromeOS and Windows. Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The Guardian

Top quality hardware aside, anyone familiar with a Chromebook would be forgiven for thinking it was ChromeOS running on these machines. It has the familiar taskbar at the bottom, Chrome-based web apps and access to Android apps.

But the software is essentially Android underneath, which means getting it up and running is just like setting up an Android phone: scan the QR code with your phone, enter a passcode and transfer your apps and accounts. It is all done and dusted in about four minutes, which is faster than setting up a modern Windows 11 machine even if you know all the shortcuts.

Access to the full gamut of Android apps is the Googlebook’s biggest strength and its greatest weakness. Practically any app you have on your phone can be installed and run on the laptop. But almost all those phone apps are just that, mobile versions, with most not even aware that they are not installed on a phone.

Those that have at least some tailoring to the laptop form come in a few different types, categorised by Google broadly under “compatible with desktop”, which means they should support mouse and keyboard controls; “optimised for desktop”, which means they should scale properly to the laptop’s display; and “made for desktop”, which are a handful of Android apps redesigned with the laptop in mind.

Only the last category really seems to make any difference to the quality of the app, and even then most of them are still not of the same calibre as their equivalents found on Windows or macOS.
A screenshot of Googlebook OS showing the Google Calendar app.
View image in fullscreen
Google Calendar can only show one account at a time, which means my schedule looks free lacking any of my work meetings. Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The Guardian
Even Google’s apps are a mixed bag. Google Calendar can only show one account at any one time, so you can’t see your personal, work and shared calendars on one screen like you can on Android.
Google Docs starts as its own app, but when you actually open a document it just becomes another Chrome window hidden behind the Chrome logo on the task bar, not the Docs logo.

The Files app shows your Google Drive files, but you can’t pin locations to the side bar to quickly access your commonly used folders, making it a time-consuming dig through endless folders to find things each time.

Even the Chrome browser is not quite up to par with its Windows or macOS counterpart, lacking features such as split-screen tabs, the auto-hiding vertical tab bar or the ability to have multiple profiles, such as a personal and work account.

Google has an app-gap problem and one that will only be solved if developers are convinced Googlebook OS is going to take off and be worth spending time and money making better apps for.
Bring your Android phone into your Googlebook
Overlapping screens show a phone app launcher, the Guardian app, and a Files window.
View image in fullscreen
You can see you phone’s apps (left), cast them (centre) and view your phone’s files (right). Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The Guardian

The other big selling point is deep integration with your Android phone. Google calls this “better together”, which is a collection of features that mirror capabilities of iPhones with Macs or Microsoft’s Link to Windows.

Some of the features are like magic. You can search the files on your phone straight from the Files app on the laptop without plugging it in, see your notifications from your phone, continue tasks on your laptop from your phone and even use apps cast from your phone.

As useful as these features sound, many are not up to scratch. Streaming apps from your phone is so slow that I feel as though I can type entire sentences before they appear on screen in chat apps, and it is restricted to one app at a time. If you click on a synced notification from your phone, it will open in a cast app, even if you have the full app installed on your Googlebook. Even viewing files on your phone from the laptop is irritatingly slow.
The only apps I’ve reliably managed to get to appear with the ability to continue from where I was are Google Docs and Chrome on the phone.

It also took me two hours of troubleshooting to get an up-to-date Google Pixel 11 Pro to actually connect with the Googlebooks, despite using the phone to set them up in the first place.
Gemini
A browser shows a chat assistant popup with suggested prompts over a Zelda game webpage.
View image in fullscreen
Wiggle the cursor to invoke Gemini and select text or images to ask questions or perform tasks on them. Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The Guardian

The other big selling point for Google is its Gemini integration into Googlebook OS. The Gemini app is just like it is on macOS and Windows. But it is the Magic Pointer feature, which appears when you wiggle the mouse to click or highlight something on your screen to send it to Gemini, that is the most novel.

You can use it to get Gemini to summarise text, explain something, search for things or generally chat. But I often hit a road block, such as Gemini refusing to generate images or saying it cannot add a date into my calendar in the mode Magic Cursor opens, which oddly isn’t within the desktop Gemini app. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, and it is simply not joined up.

Magic Cue has been imported from Google’s Pixel phones, which is meant to pop up with helpful information such as calendar availability or a location in maps when you highlight a date or a place in a chat or email. But unlike on a Pixel phone, I have yet to get it to successfully activate in two weeks of testing.

Google’s super-charged voice dictation system called Rambler, also from the recent Pixels, does at least work as described. Press the dictation key and just speak naturally. Rambler will condense your speech into concise sentences removing filler words and errors.
Verdict
Googlebooks are full of excellent ideas about how a modern laptop should work. The hardware of the Acer and Asus machines I’ve tested is top notch, but the software just isn’t ready for prime time.
When it works it’s great, but it is filled with limitations that might be acceptable on a super-cheap laptop but never on a £1,000 premium machine.

Chrome is not as good as it is on a Mac or Windows PC. Google’s various apps are generally better on an Android phone and the third-party app ecosystem is a mess of poorly optimised mobile apps. Even the best desktop-optimised Android apps pale by comparison to their counterparts on Windows or macOS.
The Android phone-linking system should be the killer feature, but it is partly broken or simply not up to scratch. Even the Gemini integration is flakey.
Most of the Google-specific issues and software bugs are eminently fixable. But the app gap will take serious time, effort and money to convince third-party developers to fix.
Unless you want to spend at least £1,000 to be a beta tester, your money is better spent elsewhere for now.

Googlebooks have only been around for a little over a month, but Google is already looking beyond traditional laptops. The company has confirmed that detachable Googlebooks are on the way, meaning we could soon see devices that work as both a tablet and a laptop without carrying two separate gadgets.

The announcement came during the Android Dev Summit 2026, where Google outlined its plans to expand the Googlebook lineup beyond the clamshell and convertible designs currently available. While the company hasn't revealed an official launch date or shown any hardware, an earlier leak suggests Lenovo could be the first manufacturer to bring one to market.
Where Googlebooks go next

Googlebooks are finally breaking away from the laptop design

Google launched its first five Googlebooks with a fairly familiar approach. Four of them, from Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo, are conventional laptops. The Acer Googlebook 14 is the only exception, offering a 360-degree hinge that lets you fold the screen backward and use it as a tablet. However, there's a big difference between folding a laptop into tablet mode and actually removing its keyboard. That's where Google's next wave of devices comes in.
Trying out the HP Googlebook at Snapdragon Summit Hands On Featured Image
Trying out the HP Googlebook at Snapdragon Summit Varun Mirchandani / Digital Trends

Interestingly, Lenovo might already have something in the works. An Android Headlines leak pointed to a Googlebook tablet with a detachable keyboard and a built-in kickstand, much like Microsoft's Surface devices. The leaked hardware also reportedly features Google's Glowbar near the camera, although its exact functionality remains unclear. We still don't know much, including the specifications, pricing, and whether Lenovo will actually be first to launch. But Google's latest confirmation makes it clear that detachable devices are officially part of its plans.
Could Googlebook OS become the future of Android tablets?

The bigger story here is what Google's expansion could mean for Android tablets. Googlebook OS is built on Android, but it's designed to offer a more desktop-like computing experience. Bringing it to detachable tablets could give users a device that's comfortable for watching videos and browsing the web, while still handling more demanding productivity tasks.
Hp Googlebook logo featured hands on
Varun Mirchandani / Digital Trends

That said, Google still has some work to do. The current software allows fullscreen apps to run in portrait orientation, but important parts of the interface, including the home screen, app drawer, and Overview, remain restricted to landscape mode. That's hardly ideal for a device designed to be used without a keyboard. It also raises an interesting question about Google's long-term tablet strategy. If Googlebook OS eventually offers a better desktop experience, where does that leave premium tablets running regular Android? With detachables officially on the roadmap, the line between Android tablets and Googlebooks is about to get a lot thinner.

Компанія Google заграє з ринком десктопних ОС у формі недорогих ноутбуків Chromebook вже понад 15 років. Й хоча гучних медійних успіхів за цей час майже не трапилося, певна популярність таких лептопів все ж беззаперечна. Можливо, зустріти Chromebook у кав'ярні буде вкрай складно. Проте навчальні заклади та бізнес відчутно активніше звернули увагу на недорогі ноутбуки з нескладною ОС, якій не так і багато потрібно для комфортної роботи.

Втім, маючи надпопулярну систему Android, Google все ж хочеться більшого. Й новою спробою краще показати себе у світі ноутбуків має новинка Googlebook. Цього тижня стартували передзамовлення перших версій таких ноутбуків. Що це таке й у чому основні особливості — розбираємося у цій статті.
Це ж ребрендинг Chromebook, правда?

Ні. Тут як реалізація, так і сама ідея цікавіші. В основі закладено не просто "просунутий Chrome", а модифіковану версію Android, яка має краще адаптуватися для роботи у форматі ноутбука, а не смартфона. Тобто й напрацювання ChromeOS не були зайвими. Ба більше, до самих пристроїв більше вимог, ніж до Chromebook. Якщо останні орієнтуються на бюджетний ринок, то Googlebook — преміальніший та потужніший варіант.
Introducing Googlebook

Для початку компанія вирізняє п'ять ключових моментів: "хардвер", ШІ, "Краще разом", застосунки та ігри, а також безпеку. І тут одразу варто зауважити, що сама Google наразі не випускає такі ноутбуки самостійно, а працює над "софтом". Тим часом пристрої забезпечать партнерські компанії. В купі фінальний результат планує наступне.
Основне про концепцію Googlebook та операційної системи

"Хардвер" передбачає використання преміальних матеріалів корпусу на кшталт алюмінію, карбону, магнію тощо. Логічним доповненням є якісний дисплей, гарні маніпулятори, динаміки, необхідні порти. Своєрідними "розпізнавальними знаками" стануть Glowbar (для початку буде показувати лише рівень заряду, інших функцій наразі не вигадали) на верхній кришці та клавіша G Key (на кшталт Win для Windows).

А разом із цим очікуйте й непоганої продуктивності, адже Googlebook пропонуватимуть рішення від Intel рівня Core Ultra третього покоління та Snapdragon X Elite, а пізніше планується варіант від MediaTek. Базові накопичувачі від 256 ГБ та від 16 ГБ оперативної пам'яті теж обов'язкові (хоча не факт, що у майбутньому не буде варіантів з 8-12 ГБ, але це вже суб'єктивна думка).
Лептопи мусять бути легкими, демонструвати конкурентну автономність, мати біометричні датчики для швидкого розблокування… Тобто вимоги дійсно доволі високі. Як і ціни. Але про них трошки пізніше.

Звісно ж на своїй відведеній сторінці Googlebook описується як пристрій Designed for Gemini Intelligence, бо куди ж нині без ШІ, правда? Але тут не йдеться про шалену продуктивність для локальних моделей, а радше маються на увазі звичні для Android функції, які інтегровано й у нову систему.

Тобто виділивши дату Gemini запропонує створити запис у календарі, з функцією Cursor можна "струснути" мишею та отримати певний аналог Circle to Search, є голосова чи текстова версія чата, "розумний" пошук, генерація плагінів для браузера тощо. Певно, якісь з функцій працюватимуть трошки швидше, ніж на смартфонах, але все ж. Так і через браузер чи окремі застосунки ніщо не заважатиме користуватися альтернативами. Проте Gemini у конкретно цьому випадку буде нативним варіантом на рівні системи, як Siri AI в Apple чи Copilot у Windows.

Куди цікавішою є синхронізація з Android-смартфоном. Причому тут вона реалізована, теоретично, краще за те, що пропонує iOS у зв'язці з macOS. За дуже схожим принципом, користувач може почати певну дію на смартфоні й потім підхопити її на лептопі, продовживши з того ж місця (адже іноді бувають електронні листи чи замовлення у магазині, які зі смартфона "ну, ніяк не зробити"). Також між смартфоном та ноутбуком буде повна синхронізація файлів (яка наразі невідомо, як саме організована) та можливість дзеркального відображення застосунків Cast My Apps, якщо щось є у користувача лише на смартфоні.

І про застосунки та ігри: Google Play Store обов'язково буде присутнім і в нових лептопах. Соціальні мережі, стримінг відео та музики, деякі застосунки на кшталт Canva, Adobe чи CapCut, Notion, Fantastical… Навіть GeForce Now є. Заразом у маркеті можна буде побачити окремі позначки для програм, які також оптимізовано під десктопний формат.
Googlebook OS може стати хорошим варіантом для Android-розробників, адже тестувати ПЗ можна буде практично без емуляції.

Притаманно одній компанії з офісом у Купертіно, тут Google також воліли не забути про безпеку, тому в хайлайтах це згадується окремим пунктом. Йдеться про два складники: швидкий доступ за допомогою біометрії, що вже залежатиме від конкретної моделі та її вартості, а також модуль безпеки Titan C, який відповідає за охорону особистих даних, паролів тощо.
Бонуси

Охочих першими випробувати Googlebook OS потішать підписками на строк від трьох місяців до року. Перший варіант надасть доступ до YouTube Premium, Adobe Premiere, Photoshop та Lightroom, Bandlab та CapCut. А протягом року можна буде користуватися Google AI Pro з 5 ТБ у "хмарі", Luminar та GeForce NOW.

Таким чином новим користувачам вдасться не лише випробувати окремі застосунки для роботи, творчості та розваг, але й встигнути до них звикнути. А там і що більше використання, то глибша інтеграція сервісів… Словом, "пробники" дійсно непогані, якщо працюватимуть добре.

Додатковим заохоченням вказують план у 10 років апдейтів. Не факт, що у багатьох користувачів лептопи загалом стільки триматимуться. Але буде дійсно цікаво подивитися, як Google втілить такий план підтримки (тим паче ми всі знаємо, як легко та швидко саме ця компанія вміє поховати продукт, якщо щось йде не за планом; а тут ризики такого чималенькі).
Перша п'ятірка експериментаторів

Вище я згадував, що Google не береться робити Googlebook власними силами. І можна було б подумати, що буде схожа історія зі смартфонами Google Nexus, які у різні часи випускалися кількома партнерами, й іноді двома різними за раз. Проте тут компанії вдалося здивувати з імплементацією — таких партнерських пристроїв буде п'ять, й усі від різних виробників та з відчутною різницею у вартості, а місцями й можливостями.
Серед сміливців є такі компанії, як Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP та Lenovo. Всі мають мінімум по 16 ГБ ОЗП, 512-гігабайтні накопичувачі, троє з процесорами Intel та двоє із Qualcomm. І майже всі 14-дюймові.

After a protracted wait, the first wave of Googlebooks is now official. Having spent a brief period testing, here’s what it’s like to use one.

I didn’t quite spend as much time with the software as my colleague Abner, so for a full set of impressions on these laptops running Googlebook OS, please read his extensive thoughts. This is a little more focused on the hardware side, with a sprinkle of software.

The good news right up top: My initial worries have almost completely been washed away, save a few minor complaints about two specific devices; there’s more here to like than I ever expected. Notice I said “almost” as there are still concerns in the back of my mind, but despite lots of, I guess, negativity surrounding and preceding this launch, the entire lineup of Googlebooks has exceeded my fairly low expectations.
For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

I do believe that this is largely due to my mixed experience with various Chromebooks across the entire price spectrum, combined with the ultimately lackluster or barebones “Desktop mode” that was added to Pixel devices over the past year.

This time, we have fewer SKUs to deal with, and of the five Googlebook devices, there appear to be fewer pinch points – save the pricing. These are not going to be cheap, with prices “starting at” $899 and, in most cases, are going to be more expensive. That is likely where a portion of you are going to stop reading and just dismiss these entirely. I can completely understand why.

Without glossing over or forgiving the frankly inflated asking price, I do believe this comes with one distinct benefit. There is less compromise in quality, which is something that worried me, given the mixed history of Chromebooks and the pitfalls of the cheapest model becoming the flag-bearer for the “default” experience.
I spent around 45 minutes prodding and poking the lineup, and there are two standouts.
Right off the bat, the Dell XPS and the HP Googlebook were the most impressive launch devices here. That said, each of the five laptops has its own merits.

ASUS’ Googlebook, Lenovo’s Googlebook 15, and Acer’s Googlebook 14 offer, in my opinion, are marginally lesser but still fairly decent takes on the first wave of hardware. The Lenovo in particular takes some design cues from previous Chromebooks and pairs with a bright HDR display. It was really easy to see despite lots of glare and jostling in the testing area.
Lenovo Googlebook 15 display

I will state that I am personally not a fan of 2-in-1 laptops, but Googlebook OS, as it’s being styled, just turns the Acer model into arguably the best touchscreen laptop-tablet hybrid on the market. In fact, all of these laptops have excellent touchscreens that run at 120Hz. I was worried ahead of time that we’d get 60Hz screens, so it was very good to see a baseline of 120Hz.

Windows and ChromeOS have always struggled with touch inputs, while MacOS doesn’t allow for user interface control with your hands – or stylus. How many elite touchscreen experiences exist on a laptop? I wager until now, none. This is where Android, in my opinion, is being leveraged in the potentially best way possible. Swipes, taps, prods, it’s all just like using your phone or a tablet.

Just dipping back into a specific device in the lineup for a second, the matte display on the Acer Googlebook 14 was a great touch. It just eliminated glare almost entirely and reminded me of the recently released iPhone Duo. My only gripe was that it was covered in greasy fingerprints and smudges after a few minutes of usage.

Lenovo, ASUS, and Acer are utilizing Intel Core Ultra “Pantherlake” chips, while Dell and HP are going with the Snapdragon X Elite chipset. All come with at least 16GB of RAM for optimal performance. Some SKUs might offer up to 32GB of RAM, but my session made no mention of storage capacities, and there is no way to expand storage using external storage like a microSD card. There could be a really easy way to get people onside by offering these in future SKUs; for now, it’s business as usual.
More good news: The performance is excellent. Every Googlebook felt especially snappy. These are desktop-level chips running Android, which sort of is to be expected.

If anything, I was shocked at how responsive the experience was. It helps that each device has almost identical specifications. You can pick the laptop that suits your specific needs and still expect performance parity. Given my trepidation due to how Chromebooks have been treated by OEMs, this was very refreshing. It’s a good sign right at launch, but let’s hope Google holds more cards this time to almost force device makers to hit base specifications once cheaper models arrive.

The touchpads on all of the models are genuinely impressive. There’s some level of haptics, but MacBooks still reign supreme here. Every keyboard felt tight and responsive, and I liked stabbing away at the keys however briefly. None of the five models felt mushy or squishy under my fingers, and the layouts were instantly familiar to my battle-worn MacBook Pro battered fingertips. I didn’t have too long to test out the two unique keyboard G and odd Caps Lock keys, but they’ll no doubt take a while to get used to if you’re coming from Windows or Mac.
Lenovo Googlebook 15

We saw ahead of launch that the lightbar is a key branding differentiator on the Googlebook. Sure, it looks nice, but it didn’t seem to do much beyond, well, look kind of cool. Google is planning on opening this LED strip up to developers in the coming months, so I’m sure we’ll get various takes on notifications, DND mode, and more that I probably haven’t thought of.

Correction: XPS laptops have been sold under the “Project Sputnik” banner with Ubuntu pre-installed in a partnership with Canonical that has been in place since 2012 and has become part of the Dell XPS Developer Edition series. Mostly focused on developers, the following incorrect statement has been removed, but is kept for posterity. Apologies for any confusion caused.

Something that I hope isn’t missed here is that the XPS Googlebook from Dell is the first such laptop from the company to come without Windows pre-installed. I think, given how mediocre the Dell Chromebook line was, this feels like a real statement of intent for a product line that is widely heralded as the best alternative to a MacBook. The company wouldn’t stake the XPS line on a mediocre product. It’s a gorgeous small-form-factor laptop, and one I really hope to spend some extended time with soon.
Can Android fill in the gap Chromebooks leave behind?

There are so many question marks over the Googlebook lineup, most notably who the platform is going to suit best or how it’ll fit into someone’s existing computing lineup. Some will ship with HDMI ports; there’s no room for a single SD card slot, or at least one that I remember spotting. I’d love to know what the experience is like using a secondary display or taking that experience elsewhere.

I feel like the software is much better than I had anticipated for a launch product. Yes, we’re missing a few top-level professional tools, but the full desktop Chrome browser might dispel some pre-launch detractors. I installed an extension I use every day, and it wanted to track my cashback while I was visiting a few of my favorite online shopping haunts. That reduced some of my initial fears of mobile Chrome on a laptop form factor.
Dell XPS Googlebook
What I cannot fault is the launch hardware. It is solid.

I went in with some preconceptions likely based on some of the leaks and, I’ll be honest, a mediocre unveil during the Android Show earlier this year. The devices have done a lot of the talking, which is an interesting prospect, as they already feel like a fluid expansion of Android into a new form factor.

Right now, I am likely not the target market. I need certain pieces of software, but ask yourself: do you have one key piece of software that is locking you into your current laptop or tablet? If that is the case, you probably were never looking at making a switch to a new desktop platform on launch day anyway.

My overriding early thought is that a Googlebook is an option for someone who has no allegiance to a desktop OS, but has a strong urge for their phone to expand into a bigger, more competent portable display. That might be a tiny portion of the market, but it could also be huge given that many people still use a phone for 95% of their day-to-day tasks. I don’t have a crystal ball or next week’s lottery numbers, but we have a new operating system to choose from, and I can’t be too negative about it. Any challengers to Windows, Mac, or Linux are good in my book. We just need things to start moving fast right out of the gate.

I think back to the early era of the smartphone. I imagined being able to take my phone, plug it into a screen, and have access to everything I need or use most. If that really worked, we’d all be using Samsung DeX, but we’re all still using separate laptops and desktops instead.

The modern smartphone is a hub for payments, photos, emails, entertainment, and the “right hand” of most people. Here’s what is different: The Googlebook takes your Android phone and turns it into a laptop. Whether you want it is ultimately up to you.
